<p>
        Plugins extend a Papercusp install along five axes:
      </p>

      <table>
        <thead><tr><th>Extension point</th><th>What it adds</th><th>Plugin SDK type</th></tr></thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr><td><strong>Lifecycle hooks</strong></td><td>Code that runs at well-known host phases (frozen surface — new pipeline integrations use event-reaction rules; plugin-system-pot-port D-003)</td><td>`PluginHooks`</td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>Event-reaction rules</strong></td><td>Declarative "when X settles, fire my tool" rules over the one reaction registry — the live pipeline extension surface (§7.0)</td><td>`PluginReactionRule`</td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>UI (full-route)</strong></td><td>A complete React panel mounted at `/harness/&lt;slug&gt;` — <strong>see §8</strong></td><td>`UiContribution`</td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>API routes</strong></td><td>A Hono sub-app the runtime mounts at `/api/plugins/&lt;name&gt;/`</td><td>`PluginApiRoutes`</td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>DB schema</strong></td><td>Postgres DDL (schemaName + ddlPath, or a bare DDL-path array) applied at install under the plugin's own schema</td><td>`PluginSchemaField`</td></tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>

      <p>
        <strong>Retired axes (2026-06-12, plugin-system-pot-port D-004):</strong> <strong>Roles</strong> (`RoleDefinition` — the old orchestrator's plugin-dispatched agent roles; live roles are `AGENT_ROLES` + blueprint role prompts, and "a plugin contributes a blueprint role" is a future design, not this axis) and <strong>Routines</strong> (`RoutineDefinition` — targeted the retired `pending_events` queue; use blueprint `triggers.schedule` or event-reaction schedules). Both manifest-level `roles` and `routines` entries remain schema-tolerated as inert `array<object>` declarative data — the loader ignores them; there are no `RoleDefinition` / `RoutineDefinition` SDK types.
      </p>

      <p>
        Plugins also declare <strong>capabilities</strong> (§10) — a permission manifest that the runtime enforces at the DI boundary. Sections 7.1–7.5 below describe the substrate-level concerns that apply to every plugin regardless of which axes it extends.
      </p>

      

### 7.0 Hooking the pipeline — event-reaction rules

      <p>
        <strong>The hybrid hook model (plugin-system-pot-port-2026-06-11 D-003, ratified 2026-06-12):</strong>
        the typed <code>PluginHooks</code> fire-points that survived the run-loop retirement
        (<code>beforeMissionStart</code>, <code>onFeaturePassed</code>, <code>afterDone</code>) are
        <strong>FROZEN</strong> — they keep firing in-process for back-compat but no new typed fire-point will
        ever be added, and their invocations bypass dispatch (no audit, no capability gate). The WordPress-style
        hook bus (<code>addAction</code>/<code>addFilter</code>, the old <code>PluginHookBus</code>) is
        <strong>retired</strong> (it had zero registered consumers). New pipeline fire-points are
        <strong>event emissions only</strong>, and plugins subscribe by declaring <strong>reaction rules</strong>.
      </p>

      <p>
        The <code>PluginHooks</code> interface declares more fire-points than
        the host wires today. Of the typed surface, only
        <code>onLoad</code> and <code>restoreFromReload</code> (at init) plus
        <code>beforeMissionStart</code>, <code>onFeaturePassed</code>, and
        <code>afterDone</code> (via <code>firePluginLifecycle</code>) are
        actually invoked by the pipeline. The remaining declared hooks —
        <code>onHarnessCreated</code>, <code>onProposalAccepted</code>,
        <code>onPostOrchestrator</code>, <code>onPostWorker</code>,
        <code>onPostValidator</code>, <code>contributeOperatorSuggestions</code> —
        exist on the type but have no fire site yet; they are declared-but-not-fired.
      </p>

      <p>
        A rule is <code>{`{ id, on, when?, fire, args?, onlyOnSuccess?, capability? }`}</code> —
        declared in the manifest (<code>reactions[]</code>, the declarative subset: <code>when</code> is a
        data-match object, <code>args</code> a static object) or on the entry plugin's
        <code>reactions</code> export (function forms allowed). The host registers each into the one
        reaction registry (<code>registerReactionRule</code>) at plugin-host boot, after the tool sweep.
      </p>

      <p><strong>The capability contract</strong> (event-reaction-system D-012):</p>
      <ul>
        <li>each trigger in <code>on</code> requires a manifest capability <code>events:listen:&lt;trigger&gt;</code> — the consent surface for what the plugin watches;</li>
        <li><code>fire</code> must name one of the plugin's <strong>own</strong> projected tools (<code>&lt;plugin&gt;.&lt;verb&gt;</code>) — registration refuses foreign targets;</li>
        <li>the reaction runs through <strong>normal dispatch</strong> under a principal holding only the rule's capability (default: the fired tool's declared capability), so auth, quota, audit and the cause-chain loop guard all ride free.</li>
      </ul>

      <p>
        <strong>What a rule can trigger on:</strong> any tool invocation observed at the dispatcher
        (e.g. <code>work_items:complete</code>, <code>work_items:claim</code>), any plugin-emitted event
        (the WASM event sink and <code>plugins:fire_event</code> feed the same matcher), and the
        <strong>pipeline event vocabulary</strong> the live DBOS pipeline emits
        (<code>lib/events/pipeline-events.ts</code>):
      </p>

      <table>
        <thead><tr><th>Reaction trigger key</th><th>`events:await` key</th><th>Fires when</th></tr></thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr><td>`pipeline:launch`</td><td>`pipeline:launch:&lt;slug&gt;`</td><td>a harness run is launched</td></tr>
          <tr><td>`pipeline:step-start`</td><td>`pipeline:step-start:&lt;slug&gt;:&lt;feature&gt;:&lt;role&gt;`</td><td>a spine role dispatch is starting</td></tr>
          <tr><td>`pipeline:step-done`</td><td>`pipeline:step-done:&lt;slug&gt;:&lt;feature&gt;:&lt;role&gt;`</td><td>a spine role dispatch finished (payload: exitCode, durationMs, runId)</td></tr>
          <tr><td>`pipeline:done`</td><td>`pipeline:done:&lt;slug&gt;:&lt;feature&gt;`</td><td>a feature pipeline finalized DONE</td></tr>
          <tr><td>`pipeline:escalate`</td><td>`pipeline:escalate:&lt;slug&gt;:&lt;feature&gt;`</td><td>a feature pipeline finalized ESCALATE (payload: reason)</td></tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>

      <p>
        The work-items lifecycle additionally emits awaited events
        (<code>work-item:claimed:&lt;id&gt;</code>, <code>work-item:blocked:&lt;id&gt;</code>,
        <code>work-item:done:&lt;id&gt;</code>, <code>work-item:unblocked:&lt;id&gt;</code>) — reaction rules
        trigger on the <em>tools</em> (<code>work_items:claim</code> / <code>set_state</code> /
        <code>complete</code>), while agents sleep on the exact keys via <code>events:await</code>. One
        emission serves reactions, awaits and UI simultaneously; registered plugin rules are inspectable via
        <code>plugins:runtime_status</code> (<code>reactionRules</code>) and <code>events:graph</code>.
      </p>

### 7.1 Inter-plugin dependencies



      <p>
        Plugins frequently rely on services or tools declared by other
        plugins. The manifest carries this dependency as plugin-slug
        metadata so lock-resolve can build a dependency graph at
        Cupboard install time.
      </p>

      <p>
        Today `requires` is a bare array of plugin slug strings (hard
        dependencies, used by `papercusp install` / `papercusp plugin
        install` to build the lock-resolve graph), with a sibling
        `recommends` array for soft dependencies — surfaced to the user
        during install but never auto-installed. There is no
        name→version-range object form and no per-entry `{ version,
        optional }` shape; both fields are arrays of slugs like
        `"@org/dep-plugin"`. (The manifest's top-level is
        `additionalProperties: false`, so only schema-known keys are
        accepted.)
      </p>

      ```json
// papercusp.json:
{
  "name": "shareholder-briefings",
  "version": "1.2.0",
  // Hard dependencies — slugs lock-resolve includes in the graph.
  "requires": ["@org/audit-log"],
  // Soft dependencies — surfaced at install, never auto-installed.
  "recommends": ["@org/papercup"]
  // ...
}
```

      <p>
        Note: there is no implemented version-range dependency resolver
        or `api.hasPlugin(name)` presence-check API today — `requires`
        and `recommends` are schema-tolerated metadata that lock-resolve
        reads to order installs, not a runtime semver gate. The
        per-version-range resolution, cascading-uninstall, and
        `--orphan` behaviors described in earlier drafts are design
        intent tracked in the plugin-system plans, not shipped code.
      </p>

      <p><strong>Runtime version pinning.</strong> Independently of
      plugin-to-plugin deps, every manifest declares the substrate
      runtime semver range it was built against, via the
      <code>papercusp</code> field:</p>

      ```json
// papercusp.json:
{
  // ...
  "papercusp": "^0.1.0"   // refuses to load outside this range
}
```

      <p>
        This is the same versioning shape as service ABI pinning
        (§8.4.1), but at the runtime level. The loader runs
        <code>satisfies(PAPERCUSP_RUNTIME_VERSION, manifest.papercusp)</code>
        on every load and rejects out-of-range plugins, catching the case
        where a plugin built against an old runtime would otherwise hit
        subtle API drift bugs. (<code>PAPERCUSP_RUNTIME_VERSION</code> is
        <code>0.1.1</code> today.)
      </p>

      <p>
        A separate <code>protocol</code> field pins the plugin
        <strong>wire-protocol</strong> version, independent of the
        runtime release cycle so hooks can evolve without bumping the
        whole runtime. It is enforced identically at load: the loader
        runs <code>satisfies(PROTOCOL_VERSION, manifest.protocol)</code>
        and refuses out-of-range plugins. <code>PROTOCOL_VERSION</code>
        is fixed at <code>1.0.0</code> today; future bumps will refuse
        loads from plugins that don't declare a compatible range.
      </p>

      

### 7.2 Plugin lifecycle — enable / disable

      <p>
        A plugin lives on disk under
        <code>~/.papercusp/global-plugins/&lt;slug&gt;/</code> (installed by
        the Cupboard git-clone above, or symlinked for local dev). Its
        runtime presence is binary per harness: <strong>enabled</strong>
        or <strong>disabled</strong>. There is no six-state machine and
        no per-plugin runtime <code>quarantined</code>/<code>updating</code>/<code>uninstalling</code>
        state tracked in code today — those, along with a crash circuit
        breaker and a transition audit log, are design intent in the
        plugin-system plans, not shipped substrate.
      </p>

      <table>
        <thead><tr><th>State</th><th>Meaning</th><th>Hooks fire?</th><th>UI mounted?</th></tr></thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>disabled</strong></td>
            <td>On disk under <code>global-plugins/&lt;slug&gt;/</code> but not wired into a harness. Config and any DB schema are retained.</td>
            <td>No</td>
            <td>No</td>
          </tr>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>enabled</strong></td>
            <td>Wired into the harness: tools projected, reaction rules registered, typed hooks live, UI route mounted at <code>/harness/&lt;slug&gt;</code>.</td>
            <td>Yes</td>
            <td>Yes</td>
          </tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>

      <p>
        The CLI wires both transitions:
        <code>papercusp plugin enable &lt;slug&gt; [--harness &lt;slug&gt;]</code>
        records the manifest's capabilities as grants for the target
        harness (after consent) and brings the plugin into the host;
        <code>papercusp plugin disable &lt;slug&gt; [--harness &lt;slug&gt;]</code>
        unwires it. (A <code>quarantined</code>/<code>withdrawn</code>
        concept does exist, but only at the <em>Cupboard lock/version
        layer</em> — <code>papercusp lock upgrade-pin</code>/<code>upgrade-all</code>
        operate over withdrawn or quarantined <em>package versions</em>,
        not a per-plugin runtime circuit-breaker.)
      </p>

      <p><strong>Hot-reload state.</strong> When a plugin reloads (a file
      change in dev, a config edit), the host can preserve in-flight
      state across the swap. If the manifest opts in
      (<code>hotReload: {`{ preserveState: true }`}</code>), the host
      calls the plugin's <code>getStateForReload(ctx)</code> before
      unloading and <code>restoreFromReload(ctx, state)</code> after the
      new module's <code>init()</code> — before any other hook. The
      stashed value (JSON, ≤ 64 KiB, keyed by plugin + harness) lives in
      <code>harness_shared.plugin_reload_state</code> (Migration 055).</p>



### 7.3 Host hook-error handling

      <p>
        Plugins fail. The host must not let one plugin's bug take down a
        harness run. The typed-hook invoker
        (<code>firePluginLifecycle</code>) wraps each handler call in
        try/catch: a throw is caught, logged to the harness run log
        (<code>hook "&lt;name&gt;" threw: &lt;message&gt;</code>), and the
        pipeline continues. The throw never propagates to the host's main
        loop.
      </p>

      <p>
        That is the whole of the shipped fault-isolation story for typed
        hooks today — <strong>catch, log, continue</strong>. There is no
        throw/timeout counting, no per-fault-class threshold, no
        quarantine transition, and no audit row. The per-plugin crash
        circuit breaker (5-throws-in-60s thresholds, handler eviction,
        a <code>circuitBreaker</code> manifest field) described in earlier
        drafts is unbuilt design intent: there is no
        <code>circuitBreaker</code> key in the SDK manifest type or the
        JSON schema (whose top-level is <code>additionalProperties:
        false</code>), so a manifest declaring one is rejected outright.
      </p>

      <p>
        Reaction rules (§7.0) are the path that <em>does</em> get the full
        substrate treatment — they run through normal dispatch, so auth,
        quota, audit, and the cause-chain loop guard all apply. New
        fault-tolerance work targets that surface, not the frozen typed
        hooks.
      </p>



### 7.4 Failure-mode taxonomy

      <p>
        The implemented substrate behavior for the failure classes that
        exist in code today:
      </p>

      <table>
        <thead>
          <tr><th>Failure</th><th>Substrate behavior</th><th>What the plugin author does about it</th></tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>Capability missing / revoked at call</strong></td>
            <td>The DI proxy / dispatch refuses the call — the capability AND-check fails (§10).</td>
            <td>Declare the capability in the manifest; wrap optional calls in try/catch and degrade gracefully.</td>
          </tr>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>Typed hook handler throws</strong></td>
            <td>Caught and logged to the run log; the pipeline continues (§7.3). No counter, no eviction, no audit row.</td>
            <td>Read the run log; keep hook bodies defensive — they are advisory, not for heavy lifting.</td>
          </tr>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>Runtime version out of range</strong></td>
            <td>The loader runs <code>satisfies(PAPERCUSP_RUNTIME_VERSION, manifest.papercusp)</code> and refuses to load with a one-line range-mismatch error.</td>
            <td>Bump the manifest's <code>papercusp</code> range and republish.</td>
          </tr>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>Wire-protocol version out of range</strong></td>
            <td>The loader runs <code>satisfies(PROTOCOL_VERSION, manifest.protocol)</code> and refuses to load.</td>
            <td>Bump the manifest's <code>protocol</code> range to include the host's <code>PROTOCOL_VERSION</code>.</td>
          </tr>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>Tool / handler cross-validation fails</strong></td>
            <td>The loader rejects the plugin at load: every manifest tool needs a handler, no orphan handlers, and each tool's capabilities must subset the plugin's declared set.</td>
            <td>Keep <code>papercusp.json</code> <code>tools[]</code> and the exported handler map in sync (or use <code>getDynamicTools</code>).</td>
          </tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>

      <p>
        The richer taxonomy from earlier drafts — per-hook deadlines with
        a <code>hooks:long-running</code> capability, API-route 500s into
        <code>audit.api_errors</code>, routine-fire timeouts into
        <code>routine_fires</code>, transactional migration rollback, UI
        slot-id collision resolution, and the
        <code>audit.plugin_errors</code>/<code>audit.install_attempts</code>
        tables — describes substrate that does not exist in code. None of
        those audit tables are defined, and routines are a retired axis
        (§7). Treat that list as design intent for the plugin-runtime
        roadmap, not current behavior.
      </p>

      

### 7.5 Developer experience



      <p>
        The inner loop for plugin authors determines whether the marketplace
        ever has third-party content. The substrate ships an opinionated
        dev mode aimed at sub-second iteration:
      </p>

      <p><em>Implemented (current state):</em> the shipped author commands are
      <code>papercusp plugin init &lt;name&gt; [--template &lt;slug&gt;]</code>
      (scaffold from a reference plugin — default <code>cloudflare-stack</code>),
      <code>papercusp plugin lint</code>, <code>papercusp plugin doctor</code>,
      and <code>papercusp plugin watch &lt;slug&gt;</code>. The manifest is a
      <code>papercusp.json</code> file (not a TS file); plugins symlink into
      <code>~/.papercusp/global-plugins/</code> for local dev. The
      <code>papercusp dev</code> single-command hot-reload session sketched
      below is design intent — see the
      <a href="/internal/docs/spec/plugin-quickstart">authoring quickstart</a>
      for the current workflow and the
      <a href="/internal/docs/spec/plugin-runtime-roadmap">runtime roadmap</a>
      for what shipped vs. deferred.</p>

      ```
$ papercusp dev ./my-plugin

==> Linked ./my-plugin into ~/.papercusp/installed/my-plugin/ (symlink)
==> Watching: src/**, papercusp.manifest.ts, migrations/**, public/**
==> Substrate state: my-plugin@dev (state=active, hot-reload=on)
==> http://localhost:3055/                ← substrate UI
==> http://localhost:3055/harness/my-plugin   ← your UI surface

[hot-reload] src/components/Tab.tsx changed → React Refresh applied (no remount)
[hot-reload] papercusp.manifest.ts changed → manifest revalidated; new capabilities require consent (paused)
[hot-reload] migrations/0002_add_foo.sql added → applied (foo column exists)
```

      <p><strong>Substrate guarantees in dev mode:</strong></p>

      <ul>
        <li><strong>UI components hot-swap.</strong> React Fast Refresh
        is preserved across the substrate-plugin boundary. Component
        state survives unless the export shape changes.</li>
        <li><strong>Hook handler swaps.</strong> Editing a handler's body
        replaces the registered function on next file save. In-flight
        handler calls continue with the old function; the next fire
        uses the new one.</li>
        <li><strong>Service ABI mismatches surface immediately</strong>
        as a substrate banner instead of a runtime crash.</li>
        <li><strong>Schema migrations auto-apply</strong> on file change.
        New `up.sql` files run in order; new `down.sql` siblings allow
        the substrate to reverse a migration when the file is reverted
        (`papercusp dev --no-auto-migrate` opts out).</li>
        <li><strong>Capability changes pause the plugin</strong> with a
        single-line consent prompt rather than auto-granting in dev.
        The author must approve, just as users will. This catches the
        "works on my machine, fails on user install" failure mode.</li>
        <li><strong>Routines fire at 10× normal cadence</strong> when
        `papercusp dev --fast-routines` is set, so cron jobs are
        observable in a 5-minute session instead of waiting an hour.</li>
      </ul>

      <p><strong>What dev mode does not do:</strong></p>

      <ul>
        <li>It does not bypass capability checks. A plugin that needs
        `secrets:read:FOO` in production needs it in dev too.</li>
        <li>It does not change the wire format of any DI service or
        hook payload. What works in dev works in install — modulo
        environment differences.</li>
        <li>It does not auto-publish. Publishing is always
        `papercusp publish`, an explicit user action.</li>
      </ul>

      <p><strong>Plugin SDK scaffolding.</strong></p>

      ```
$ papercusp plugin init my-plugin --template cloudflare-stack

==> Creating ./my-plugin/
    package.json
    papercusp.json
    index.cjs
    provision/setup.sh
    README.md
    ...

==> Done. Next:
    cd my-plugin && papercusp plugin lint
```

      <p>
        <code>papercusp plugin init</code> copies an existing reference
        plugin (default <code>cloudflare-stack</code>) and rewrites every
        reference to the new slug; <code>--template &lt;slug&gt;</code> picks
        a different starter and <code>--from-path &lt;dir&gt;</code> forks a
        local checkout. Because the scaffold is a real first-party plugin
        under <code>libs/papercusp/plugins/</code>, the output is verifiable
        from source.
      </p>
